posts.topic: sitting at the supper table until the peas were gone
posts.on_image: YOU'LL SIT THERE TILL THOSE PEAS ARE GONE.
posts.caption: Peas were the one vegetable my brother Gary could not get down, and Dad knew it. The rest of us cleared the table and went in to watch Bonanza, and Gary stayed put with a plate of peas going cold and gray. Dad sat across from him with his coffee and didn't say a word. Gary tried hiding a few under the mashed potatoes. He tried mashing the rest flat with his fork so the plate looked emptier. Around nine o'clock Mom slipped in, covered the plate with wax paper and set it in the Frigidaire, and that was the night Gary learned peas taste even worse for breakfast.
posts.first:
My sister Patty used to slide hers into her milk glass one at a time, and it worked for almost a whole year. Then Mom poured out the last of the milk one night and found eleven peas sitting at the bottom. Patty drank her milk at the counter after that, where Mom could see her.

posts.topic: the regifted fruitcake that made the rounds
posts.on_image: NOBODY EVER ATE THE FRUITCAKE. IT JUST MOVED TO A NEW HOUSE. EVERY CHRISTMAS.
posts.caption: Aunt Velma mailed us a fruitcake the first Christmas after she moved to Terre Haute, wrapped in foil inside a round red tin. Mom thanked her, set it on top of the Frigidaire, and the next December she wrapped it right back up for the Hendersons across the street. It was heavy enough to prop a door open, and it had those green cherries nobody could name. Two years later it came back to us from cousin Butch's wife, same tin, same dent in the lid. Dad said it was the best traveled thing in the family. As far as I know it is still out there somewhere, looking exactly the same.
posts.first:
Grandma Edna was the only person I ever knew who actually liked fruitcake. She soaked hers in a little brandy and kept it wrapped in a dish towel in the bread box until New Year's. She'd cut you a slice as thin as a playing card and watch you eat every bite.

posts.topic: waiting on Mom in the department store (hiding inside the clothes rack)
posts.on_image: MOM: I'LL ONLY BE A MINUTE. / TWO HOURS LATER
posts.caption: Every Saturday Mom had a list for Montgomery Ward, and every Saturday she promised it would be quick. My job was to stand next to her while she held up blouses and turned the tags over to look at the price. After about the first hour I gave up and crawled inside one of those round clothes racks. It was quiet in there, like a little tent made of coats, and it smelled like new wool and floor wax. I could hear her out there talking to the saleslady about a sweater for Aunt Lucille. When she finally said my whole name out loud in the middle of the store, I knew we were going home.
posts.first:
The best rack was the one with the long winter coats, because you could sit all the way down and nobody could see your shoes. My brother Ronnie fell asleep in one at Sears once. Mom said she aged ten years in the forty minutes it took to find him.

posts.topic: bundled into a snowsuit so stiff your arms stuck out
posts.on_image: I CAN'T PUT MY ARMS DOWN.
posts.caption: The first good snow of the year meant Mom zipped me into a quilted red snowsuit that had already been through two cousins. Then came the rubber boots over two pairs of socks, then the mittens, then a scarf wound around my face until only my eyes showed. By the time she pulled the stocking cap down, my arms stuck straight out like a scarecrow and I couldn't bend at the middle. I walked out to the yard like a little tin man. Ten minutes later I tipped over in the drift by the garage and lay there like a turtle on its back until my sister Darlene came out and rolled me over. Then I had to go to the bathroom.
posts.first:
Our snowsuits had nylon pants that went swish swish with every step, so Mom could hear us coming from the other end of the block. When they got wet they froze stiff, and she stood them up on the heat register to thaw like two little headless kids. The whole kitchen smelled like wet wool till supper.

posts.topic: the crocheted lady toilet roll cover
posts.on_image: EVERY BATHROOM HAD A CROCHETED LADY STANDING GUARD OVER THE SPARE ROLL.
posts.caption: Grandma Nell made them by the dozen out of leftover yarn and sold them at the church bazaar for a dollar apiece. Ours wore a pink ruffled skirt and a little crocheted bonnet, with a plastic doll head on top whose eyes clicked shut when you tipped her over. The skirt was the toilet paper. Everybody knew it and nobody ever said so. When company came you could hear them in there trying to figure out how to get the roll out without taking her apart. Mom finally kept a plain roll on the back of the tank where people could find it, and the lady just stood there looking pretty until about 1984.
posts.first:
The one at my great aunt's house in Muncie was a bride, all white yarn with a little veil, and she sat on that tank for thirty years. I was a little scared of her. Her eyes stayed open no matter which way you tipped her.
